---
title: "Vaccines couldn't save the border: what a COVID model tells us about quarantine under Delta"
author: "Urvi Joshi"
date: "2026-10-10"
categories: [public health, COVID-19, policy, data]
bibliography: references.bib
---

When vaccines started rolling out in early 2021, governments across Australia, New Zealand and China allowed themselves a rare moment of optimism. If travellers were vaccinated before they arrived, surely the expensive, politically painful machinery of hotel quarantine could finally be wound back?

A 2022 paper in *Science Advances* by Zachreson and colleagues ran the numbers. Their answer was blunt: under the Delta variant, vaccines restored almost none of the headroom that policymakers were counting on [@zachreson2022].

---

## The problem: you can't price a probability

Border quarantine is a strange policy tool. Its costs are easy to see — stranded citizens, capped arrivals, damaged aviation and tourism industries. Its benefits, though, are a probability: the chance that a dangerous pathogen *doesn't* reach the community. Pricing something that doesn't happen is hard, and no government was willing to state an absolute risk tolerance.

The Zachreson model sidesteps this neatly. Rather than inventing a risk threshold, it asks: *what level of risk did countries already accept in 2020?* That baseline — unvaccinated travellers, ancestral virus strain, 14-day quarantine — becomes the yardstick. Every result in the paper is then expressed as a ratio to that accepted standard. If a new arrangement lands at 1.0, it's no riskier than before. If it lands at 0.03, countries could handle thirty times the arrivals for the same community exposure.

The World Health Organization framed this kind of trade-off explicitly as a risk-based exercise rather than a fixed rule [@who2021]. The Zachreson model is one of the few attempts to actually do the arithmetic.

---

## The analysis: what the model found

### The facility model

The simulation tracks a single 100-bed quarantine hotel: 50 travellers arriving per week, 1% infected on arrival, staffed by 20 workers. Travellers stay 14 days minimum, with PCR tests on days 3 and 12. Arrivals are held in close-contact groups of four — a key structural detail, as we'll see.

When someone infectious slips through into the community, those events are fed into a second model that simulates how an outbreak spreads through the general population. The output the paper reports is how long it takes before a community cluster of more than five cases becomes 95% likely. The longer that horizon, the better the quarantine system is doing.

### Vaccines offset Delta — exactly and only that

@fig-efficacy shows the core result. The x-axis is the basic reproduction number R₀ — a measure of how contagious a variant is. Delta's R₀ was estimated at around 6 from a well-traced outbreak in Guangdong [@kang2022]. The y-axis is the vaccine efficacy against transmission needed to hold breach risk at the 2020 benchmark.

```{r}
#| label: fig-efficacy
#| fig-cap: "Vaccine efficacy against onward transmission required to hold quarantine breach risk at the pre-Delta, pre-vaccine benchmark (R₀ = 3, no vaccination). The conservative line assumes vaccinated people who are infected are as contagious as unvaccinated people; the optimistic line assumes the vaccine also reduces transmission from breakthrough cases. Source: Zachreson et al. (2022)."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

conservative <- data.frame(
  R0 = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10),
  efficacy = c(0, 20, 45, 62, 68, 72, 75, 75),
  assumption = "Conservative (main result)"
)

optimistic <- data.frame(
  R0 = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10),
  efficacy = c(0, 10, 28, 42, 48, 52, 55, 55),
  assumption = "Optimistic (sensitivity)"
)

df <- bind_rows(conservative, optimistic)
delta_band <- data.frame(xmin = 5.5, xmax = 8.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf)

ggplot(df, aes(x = R0, y = efficacy, colour = assumption, linetype = assumption)) +
  geom_rect(data = delta_band,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            fill = "#DBEAFE", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y = 90, label = "Plausible range\nfor Delta",
           colour = "#1B2A4A", size = 3.2, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Conservative (main result)" = "#1B2A4A",
                                  "Optimistic (sensitivity)" = "#2E6DA4")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Conservative (main result)" = "solid",
                                    "Optimistic (sensitivity)" = "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 3:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Basic reproduction number (R₀)",
       y = "Vaccine efficacy required",
       colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F7F6F2", colour = NA)
  )
```

At Delta's R₀ of 6, a vaccine must be more than **60% effective against transmission** just to hold breach risk where it was before Delta and before vaccines. That's a demanding bar — and it's the conservative estimate. The optimistic case brings the threshold down to about 40%, which is more achievable but still not easy.

Notice how the curve flattens past R₀ = 8. That's not a biological result — it's a structural one. Because arrivals are held in cohort groups of four with strict separation between groups, once an infection enters a group it has very few onward targets regardless of how transmissible it is.

### The headroom that vaccination was supposed to buy

@tbl-scenarios shows the four scenarios the paper compares directly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: "Relative quarantine breach risk under four scenarios, expressed as integrated force of infection released into the community relative to the pre-Delta unvaccinated benchmark. Values from Zachreson et al. (2022)."
#| echo: false

library(knitr)

scenarios <- data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Pre-Delta, unvaccinated", "Pre-Delta, vaccinated pathway",
               "Delta, unvaccinated", "Delta, vaccinated pathway"),
  R0 = c("3", "3", "6", "6"),
  `Vaccine efficacy` = c("0%", "90%", "0%", "60%"),
  `Breach risk vs benchmark` = c("1.0 (benchmark)", "~0.03", "~3×", "~1.0"),
  `What it means` = c(
    "The risk already accepted in 2020",
    "Room for ~30× the arrivals at the same exposure",
    "Three times the breach exposure of 2020",
    "Back to exactly where 2020 was — no improvement"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(scenarios)
```

The pre-Delta vaccinated pathway was extraordinary: breach risk at 3% of benchmark means countries could theoretically have handled 30 times the arrivals for the same community exposure. Delta consumed that entire advantage. A fully vaccinated pathway under Delta lands back at almost exactly the 2020 baseline.

---

## Conclusion: the filter changes what enters, not what happens next

The finding the Zachreson paper earns is deceptively simple: a screening system's performance has to be assessed jointly with the environment it protects.

Vaccinating a quarantine hotel to the hilt still leaves an under-vaccinated population exposed, because the quarantine filter changes the rate of arrivals into the community, not what happens when they get there. Delta didn't just raise the bar for quarantine — it raised it to roughly the level already being cleared, and pocketed the surplus that vaccines had been expected to deliver.
